subject: system-design
title: Design TinyURL
summary: A URL shortener that maps a long URL to a tiny code and redirects on lookup — a small surface area hiding a sharp read-heavy, key-generation problem.

blocks.text: TinyURL takes a long URL and hands back a short code, then redirects anyone who visits the short link to the original. The whole system is essentially one giant lookup table, which makes it a favourite warm-up: the API is trivial, but generating short codes that never collide and serving redirects at scale is where the real design lives.

items: Create a short link from a long URL, and redirect from the short code to the original.
Optional custom alias and an optional expiry date on a link.
Basic click analytics — count and roughly attribute redirects.
Non-functional: extremely read-heavy, very low redirect latency, high availability.

blocks.text: Assume 100M new URLs a month and a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, so on the order of 10B redirects a month. That is a few hundred writes per second but tens of thousands of reads per second. Even a decade of links at a few hundred bytes each is only low-terabyte storage — the challenge is read throughput and latency, not capacity.

A write request generates a unique short code, stores the mapping, and returns the short URL; a read resolves the code back to the long URL and issues an HTTP redirect. The pieces are a write service and read service behind a load balancer, a key-value store holding code → long URL (partitioned by code), and a cache in front of it serving hot links from memory so most redirects never touch the store.

There are two camps. Hash the long URL (e.g. take the first few characters of an MD5) — simple, but different URLs can produce the same prefix, so you must detect and resolve collisions on every write. Or take a unique number from a counter or Snowflake-style ID generator and base62-encode it into [0-9a-zA-Z]; seven base62 characters cover over 3.5 trillion codes.

blocks.title: Why base62-of-an-ID beats hashing
blocks.text: If each code is the base62 encoding of a guaranteed-unique ID, codes are unique by construction — there is nothing to collide. Hashing maps an unbounded URL space onto a short fixed-length code, so collisions are inevitable and every write needs a check-and-retry. Uniqueness moves from runtime luck to a property of how the key is made.

A 301 (permanent) redirect lets browsers and intermediaries cache the mapping, so future clicks skip your servers entirely — great for load, terrible for analytics, since you stop seeing most clicks. A 302 (temporary) routes every click back through you, so you can count and update analytics, at the cost of serving every redirect. The choice is a direct trade between offloading traffic and observing it.

Link popularity is heavily skewed, so a cache like Redis in front of the store, keyed by short code, serves the bulk of redirects from memory. Cache-aside with a TTL works well — a miss reads the store and populates the cache, and a link's expiry naturally bounds how stale an entry can be. Counting clicks for a 302 can be fire-and-forget into an async pipeline so analytics never slow the redirect.

blocks.title: Takeaway
blocks.text: TinyURL is read-heavy lookup plus key generation. Prefer base62-of-a-unique-ID to sidestep collision handling, cache hot codes hard, and pick 301 vs 302 by whether you value offloading traffic or measuring it.
